https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: British Museum under pressure to end fossil fuel ties
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.subtitle: The Museums Association’s code could force change on ethical grounds at the institution, which signed a ten-year deal worth £50m with BP two years ago
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
The British Museum has been told to “transition away” from fossil fuel sponsorship as the umbrella body for Britain’s cultural institutions tightens its ethical guidelines on raising money.
The Museums Association’s code of ethics calls on all its members to move away from “organisations involved with environmental harm (including fossil fuels), human rights abuses and other sponsorship that does not align with the values of the museum”.
The draft code is a significant strengthening of existing rules, which date from 2015, and comes with the museum world divided on where it can source sponsorship from.
The association’s existing code merely says members should “seek support from organisations whose ethical values are consistent with those of the museum”.
The British Museum has been criticised by other national museums after agreeing in 2023 to a ten-year £50 million sponsorship deal with the energy company BP.
Maria Balshaw, the director of Tate which ended its 26-year partnership with BP in 2017, wrote last year in her book Gathering of Strangers: Why Museums Matter that she had been dismayed by the British Museum’s decision.
She said the deal came at a time when “so many UK institutions have committed to not supporting companies whose green energy work can be said to be too little and too slow, in the hope that they will be motivated to move faster”.
Earlier this year BP announced it was moving away from renewable energy investments to refocus on increasing gas and oil production.
The Science Museum, which like the British Museum is a recipient of tens of millions of pounds of public funding each year, still has partnerships with BP and the Adani Group, one of the largest coal extractors in the world.
The vast majority of cultural institutions in Britain receiving public funding have distanced themselves from fossil fuel companies in recent years.
Others, including the Royal Opera House and National Portrait Gallery — at the time run by Nicholas Cullinan who is now the British Museum director — have also ended their deals with BP.
The Museums Association’s director, Sharon Heal, said it would not be commenting until the draft code had been approved, which is scheduled to happen at its AGM next month.
The British Museum said it appreciated the work of the association and it would “balance” its financial needs and considerations against “any new guidance”.
It said: “The museum operates on public and private funding which ensures the magnificent collection stays on display to the public for centuries to come. We consider each donation or sponsorship on its own merits — in line with our policy — and as a public body have an obligation to ensure the long-term financial stability of the museum by securing funding from a number of sources.”
The association, which lobbies for the sector as well as providing grants and helping facilitate loans between institutions, has expelled members in the past for failing to follow its code of ethics.
Expulsions have usually only happened after an institution has sold some of its collection for commercial gain.
Culture Unstained, which campaigns against fossil fuel sponsorship of cultural institutions, said the “new code of ethics offers an opportunity to set a powerful new precedent, not just in the UK but internationally”.
It said if the code was adopted it would “send a clear signal that sponsors fuelling and financing climate breakdown and human rights abuses cross an ethical red line — and are no longer welcome in our museums and galleries”.
